one_liner: OpenCL GraphBLAS-style sparse linear algebra for Intel, AMD and Nvidia GPUs; on a GTX 1070 it beats CPU LAGraph/SuiteSparse on PageRank and SSSP.
what_it_does: Provides GraphBLAS-like matrices, vectors and scalars with masked mxv/vxm, mxm, masked mxm-transposed, Kronecker product, element-wise add and multiply, reductions, transpose, and row and column extraction. Operations take built-in or user-defined semiring functions. The work runs on a GPU through OpenCL 1.2, with a CPU fallback. Ready-made graph algorithms (bfs, sssp, pr, tc, each with a naive CPU reference) come with the shared library, behind a C++ API, a C API (spla.h) and the pyspla Python bindings. The interface is its own and is not the GraphBLAS C API, so LAGraph or SuiteSparse code must be rewritten to use it.
how_it_is_fast: Graph algorithms are written as masked sparse matrix-vector products over semirings and run as OpenCL kernels. For a sparse frontier, vxm uses expand-sort-compress: it counts products per row, prefix-sums the offsets, collects products, then runs a GPU sort-by-key and reduce-by-key. Masked mxv has a scalar kernel with early exit, which pulls only until a hit. User operators are pasted into the OpenCL source as #defines and functions, compiled at runtime and cached by a key, so custom semirings get fused kernels. Most of the headline gain is GPU memory bandwidth and parallelism against a 4-core CPU baseline.
when_to_use: PageRank-style iterative SpMV on a discrete GPU: the README chart shows about 7.5x to 50x over LAGraph on a 4-core i7-6700 on 12 graphs, and spla beats Gunrock on every one.
SSSP on large high-diameter graphs (road networks), where the chart shows up to about 23x (road_central) on a GTX 1070.
Code that must run on Intel, AMD and Nvidia GPUs, including integrated ones, from one OpenCL code base instead of CUDA-only GraphBLAST or cuBool.
Prototyping GraphBLAS-style algorithms with custom semirings from Python or C++, where runtime-compiled user operators matter more than peak speed.
when_not_to_use: Production use: the README says 'project under heavy development! Not ready for usage.', the CHANGELOG has no release entries, and PyPI's only pyspla release is 0.0.5 from 2022-08-17.
BFS: the chart shows about 0.7x to 3.7x, and spla is slower than LAGraph on coAuthorsCiteseer, belgium_osm, com-Orkut and indochina-2004.

Integrated GPUs with the CPU baseline on the same chip: spla loses to LAGraph on every BFS run, on most SSSP runs, and on every triangle-counting run on the Ryzen 9 7900X/GFX1036, and wins only PageRank.
Graphs larger than GPU memory: RAM-to-VRAM streaming is an open feature request (#211), so the matrix must fit on the device.
Sparse linear solvers or numerical linear algebra (factorizations, Krylov methods): spla is graph-analytics oriented and has none.

integration.form: shared lib (libspla_<arch> built with CMake; C and C++ headers; pyspla Python package)
integration.dependencies: OpenCL 1.2 runtime and drivers (Khronos headers and ICD loader vendored as submodules; Apple's OpenCL framework on macOS), robin_hood and svector (vendored, private); cxxopts and gtest only for examples and tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; CMake 3.15+; Ninja and Python 3.7+ for build.py; MSVC is the only supported compiler on Windows
integration.platforms: Linux (x64, riscv), Windows x64, macOS x64 and arm64. GPU acceleration on Intel, AMD and Nvidia through OpenCL; a CPU-only mode is available via set_force_no_acceleration.
integration.thread_safety: not documented (the library uses a global Library instance with a selected accelerator, platform, device and queue count)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — GraphBLAS-like semantics but a different C++/C/Python API from the GraphBLAS C API used by SuiteSparse and LAGraph

gotchas: The headline chart compares a GTX 1070 GPU with LAGraph on a 4-core CPU. Compiler flags, LAGraph and SuiteSparse versions and thread counts are not given, and the harness for LAGraph, GraphBLAST and Gunrock is not in the repo; only spla's examples/ (bfs, sssp, pr, tc) are.

The README text claims '1 BILLION edges ... without memory issues' and 'much faster than scipy or networkx', but no published numbers back either. The largest benchmarked graph has 302M edges (indochina-2004).
OpenCL programs are built at first use (with -cl-std=CL1.2), so the first call of each operation and type combination pays a compile cost before the cache helps; exclude warm-up from timing.
Not the same project as eth-cscs/spla (distributed GEMM), which is also catalogued; check the repo owner.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick spla over GraphBLAST or cuBool when you need non-Nvidia or integrated GPUs, or PageRank-heavy work. GraphBLAST is CUDA-only, and cuBool is CUDA-only and Boolean-only (cuBool comes from the same SparseLinearAlgebra organisation). GraphBLAST beats spla's PageRank on several graphs (belgium_osm, roadNet-CA, cit-Patents). For CPU-only or production GraphBLAS work, ALP/GraphBLAS or SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS are far more mature.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README charts compare spla on an Nvidia GTX 1070 against LAGraph (SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS) on the same machine's 4-core i7-6700, over 13 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graphs (Ubuntu 20.04). Read off the log axis: PageRank about 7.5-50x, SSSP about 1.4-23x, TC about 4-12x, BFS about 0.7-3.7x. On integrated GPUs (Intel HD 530, AMD GFX1036) spla wins only PageRank. Compiler, flags and baseline versions are not stated.
status_note: Some activity (last commit 2025-11-17, 35 stars, 10 open issues, mostly feature requests) but self-described as not ready for use, with no releases beyond a 2022 pyspla 0.0.5. MIT-licensed, so research code is free to borrow.
